summary: EAP-AKA' lets devices authenticate to mobile networks using the 3GPP Authentication and Key Agreement mechanism inside the Extensible Authentication Protocol. It differs from EAP-AKA by binding derived keys to the access network name and by using SHA-256 based hashing instead of SHA-1. This version covers both 4G and 5G deployments, and updates RFC 4187 and RFC 5448.

plainLanguage.summary: When your phone joins a mobile network, both sides prove who they are. This document describes a stronger version of that handshake, and it now works for 5G too.

questions: difference between eap-aka and eap-aka prime
subtitle: How a phone or device proves itself to a mobile network over EAP, with keys tied to the access network's name.

tldr.problem: Devices need to use 3GPP mobile-network authentication (AKA) inside EAP, but plain EAP-AKA derives keys without binding them to the access network and relies on SHA-1.
tldr.mechanism: EAP-AKA' follows EAP-AKA but adds the access network name to the key derivation, supports negotiating the key derivation function, and uses SHA-256 and HMAC-SHA-256. This version also specifies how identifiers are used in 5G.
tldr.outcome: This is the most recent, fully backwards-compatible EAP-AKA' specification, covering both 4G and 5G. It updates RFC 4187 and RFC 5448 but does not obsolete RFC 5448.

facts.label: AT_KDF
facts.value: attribute 24; value 1 is the default function

today: RFC 9048 is Informational. It updates RFC 4187 and RFC 5448 without obsoleting RFC 5448, and it is itself updated by RFC 9678.

sections.title: What EAP-AKA' Is
sections.content:
The 3GPP mobile network Authentication and Key Agreement (AKA) is how devices authenticate to mobile networks. RFC 4187 (EAP-AKA) made it usable inside the Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) framework, and RFC 5448 defined the improved EAP-AKA'. The RFC says EAP-AKA' is commonly implemented in mobile phones and network equipment, and can be used for network access via wireless LANs and, with 5G, directly to mobile networks.

RFC 9048 is the most recent specification. It does not obsolete RFC 5448, but it is the newest and fully backwards-compatible one. Its changes are modest: it points to a 5G release of the 3GPP network-name rules, specifies identifier use in 5G, defines exported parameters, tightens pseudonym generation, and adds security, privacy and pervasive monitoring discussion. The RFC states that it deliberately adds no other technical changes, because the base protocol is stable.
sections.plainLanguage: It is the secret handshake your phone does with a mobile network. This version is the newest rulebook, updated so it also covers 5G.

sections.title: How EAP-AKA' Differs From EAP-AKA
sections.content:
EAP-AKA' follows RFC 4187 in every respect except five. It uses EAP Type code 0x32 instead of 0x17; it carries the AT_KDF_INPUT attribute so both sides know the access network name; it supports key derivation function negotiation through AT_KDF; it calculates keys differently; and it uses SHA-256 and HMAC-SHA-256 instead of SHA-1 and HMAC-SHA-1.

In the exchange, the server sends an EAP-Request/AKA'-Challenge with the random challenge (AT_RAND), the authentication token (AT_AUTN), the key derivation function (AT_KDF), the network name (AT_KDF_INPUT) and a MAC. The peer checks the network name against what it observes locally, verifies the token, and replies with AT_RES and AT_MAC. The server checks both and sends EAP-Success.

For IMSI-based permanent usernames on 4G, EAP-AKA' MUST use the leading character 6 instead of 0. In 5G that leading character is not used.
sections.plainLanguage: It is the same handshake as the old one, but the network also says its name out loud and both sides use a stronger scrambling method.

sections.title: Network Name and Key Derivation Negotiation
sections.content:
The server sends the access network name in AT_KDF_INPUT (attribute 23) as a UTF-8 string built as 3GPP TS 24.302 specifies, with fields separated by colons. It MUST be non-empty. The peer MAY compare it with its own view of the name; on a mismatch its policy decides whether to warn and continue or fail, and if it continues it MUST use the name the server sent. A prefix match is allowed, so a peer that knows only FOO matches the server value FOO:BAR.

The server sends one or more AT_KDF attributes (attribute 24), most preferred first. Value 1 is the default function that uses CK' and IK'. If the peer cannot or will not use the first one, it answers with a single AT_KDF naming its choice from the offered list. The server then re-sends the challenge with that choice added at the front and the entire list retained, so the choice appears twice, and the peer MUST check that only the requested change happened.
sections.plainLanguage: The network says its name and offers a list of scrambling recipes. If your phone does not like the first recipe, it picks another one, and both sides double check nobody tampered with the list.

sections.title: Keys and Hash Functions
sections.content:
For AT_KDF value 1, the master key is MK = PRF'(IK'|CK', "EAP-AKA'"|Identity). The pseudorandom function PRF' is the same construction IKEv2 uses, built from HMAC-SHA-256. The first 1664 bits of its output are split into the encryption key K_encr, the authentication key K_aut, the re-authentication key K_re, the Master Session Key (MSK) and the Extended Master Session Key (EMSK).

CK' and IK' are derived as 3GPP TS 33.402 specifies from the AKA outputs CK and IK and the network name. The server MUST set the Authentication Management Field separation bit to 1, and the peer MUST check it. On fast re-authentication, MSK and EMSK are derived from K_re, and the network name is not allowed to change between the full and fast authentication.

AT_MAC uses HMAC-SHA-256-128, the first 16 bytes of the 32-byte HMAC-SHA-256 value. AT_CHECKCODE grows to hold a 32-byte value.
sections.plainLanguage: Both sides mix a few secrets with the network's name to make a set of fresh keys, each with its own job, like separate keys for the front door, the garage and the safe.

sections.title: Preventing Bidding Down
sections.content:
Method negotiation in EAP is insecure, so a man-in-the-middle could push both sides to the weaker EAP-AKA even though both support EAP-AKA'. To catch this, RFC 4187 is updated with the AT_BIDDING attribute (136). A server sends it in the EAP-AKA challenge; its D bit is 1 when the sender supports EAP-AKA', is willing to use it and prefers it.

If the peer also supports and prefers EAP-AKA', it treats the authentication as failed. Because the attribute is protected by EAP-AKA's integrity mechanism, an attacker cannot remove it. The RFC assumes EAP-AKA' is always stronger, so there is no protection against attackers forcing the endpoints to use EAP-AKA'.
sections.plainLanguage: If both of you know the fancy handshake but someone tricks you into using the old one, a hidden note in the old handshake gives it away and you stop.

sections.title: Identities and Privacy
sections.content:
A permanent identity such as the IMSI is easy to track, so EAP-AKA' supports privacy-friendly identifiers. It defines four username types: permanent usernames, privacy-friendly temporary usernames (such as the 5G GUTI or SUCI), pseudonym usernames and fast re-authentication usernames. Pseudonyms and fast re-authentication identities MUST be generated in a cryptographically secure way and MUST NOT contain anything that links them to a subscriber.

In 5G, the SUPI is the permanent subscriber identifier and the SUCI is a concealed form that encrypts it with public key cryptography. The SUPI MUST NOT be sent in EAP-AKA' when authenticating to a 5G network, although it is used internally in key derivation. When the AT_KDF_INPUT value has the prefix 5G:, the key derivation identity follows 3GPP TS 33.501 and has no leading 0 or 6. The RFC warns that the SUCI null scheme gives no privacy, so it is NOT RECOMMENDED where identity privacy matters.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of shouting your real name, your phone hands over a scrambled nickname that changes, so eavesdroppers cannot follow you around.

sections.title: Security Properties
sections.content:
Under the assumption that HMAC-SHA-256 is at least as secure as HMAC-SHA-1, EAP-AKA' is at least as secure as EAP-AKA. Its key derivation gives an effective strength against brute force equal to the smaller of the derived key length and the AKA base key length, 128 bits or more. The keys protecting EAP-AKA packets, the MSK and the EMSK are cryptographically separate.

Binding the network name into the keys means leaked keys are useful only for access under that name. A malicious access point cannot claim to be network Y with keys stolen from network X, and some "lying NAS" attacks are prevented. The RFC notes that no published attack violates the primary secrecy or authentication properties of AKA under its original trust model, but it describes attacks under different trust models and several privacy attacks. It also recommends a perfect forward secrecy mechanism against theft of long-term keys, and says EAP-AKA' does not provide channel bindings as RFC 3748 defines them.
sections.plainLanguage: Because the keys are tied to the network's name, a stolen key only works for that one network, like a hotel key that opens only one hotel.
